question: A phone speaker barely plays the 55 Hz low A of a bass guitar. Why do you still hear the bass line?
answer: Because the brain puts it back. A bass note is a stack of harmonics, all multiples of 55 Hz, and together they repeat 55 times a second even with the bottom one gone. The ear takes that repetition as the pitch. Bass enhancers such as Waves' MaxxBass add harmonics a small speaker can play.
move: Your senses report the pattern they infer, not only what arrives.
ask: Where am I hearing or seeing something the signal never carried?

scene.hint: A bass guitar's low A, in eight harmonics. Tap the 55 Hz bar, the one a phone can't play.

moments.name: No 55 Hz in it
moments.text: The bottom tone is gone, yet the wave still repeats every 18 ms. Same note.

moments.name: Phone speaker
moments.text: Only 220 to 440 Hz left, the range a phone plays well. Still a 55 Hz note.

moments.name: Evens only
moments.text: Now they are 110 Hz apart, and the pitch jumps an octave. The ear reads the gaps.

reference: Plack, Oxenham, Fay & Popper (eds), Pitch: Neural Coding and Perception, Springer Handbook of Auditory Research 24, 2005; Waves Audio, MaxxBass: harmonics generated so the ear perceives bass below the speaker's limit
